title: Correlation between normal character and Raman intensities of isotopologues of carbon dioxide
authors: Eduardo Suárez, Christian Ostertag-Henning, Miguel Carvajal, Renato Lemus
abstract: Previous studies on the vibrational structure of carbon dioxide isotopologues have revealed a correlation between the strength of Fermi interactions and a recently defined normal-mode parameter. In this contribution, we investigate how the Raman intensities of the most intense bands evolve across the complete series of carbon dioxide isotopologues at room temperature. To this end, we introduce a general scheme for simulating Raman intensities in linear triatomic molecules, based on the computation of the mean polarizability surface up to cubic terms for all twelve stable species. For the first time, we establish correlations between the degree of normality and the Raman transition intensities, mean polarizability derivatives, and variational Raman shift errors across the CO$_2$ isotopologue series. The observed trends are further analyzed by considering rotational contributions, which may partially account for the deviations observed in the correlations. Our study is supported by experimental Raman spectra of isotopically enriched samples and theoretical simulations. Although this study focuses on carbon dioxide, similar behavior is expected for other series of isotopologues.
summary: This paper investigates the relationship between the vibrational structure, quantified by the degree of normality ($\delta^-$), and the measurable Raman intensities across different isotopologues of $	ext{CO}_2$. Using an advanced anharmonic model, the authors establish quantitative correlations between $\delta^-$ and spectroscopic parameters. This work advances the theoretical understanding of molecular spectroscopy by linking fundamental vibrational symmetries to observable physical properties.
main_problem: To establish quantitative correlations between the degree of normality of vibrational modes and measurable spectroscopic properties, specifically Raman intensities, across a series of $	ext{CO}_2$ isotopologues.
main_result: The study successfully establishes correlations linking the degree of normality ($\delta^-$) to Raman transition intensities and mean polarizability derivatives across the $	ext{CO}_2$ isotopologue series.
method: The authors developed a general scheme to simulate Raman intensities by computing the mean polarizability surface up to cubic terms, utilizing an anharmonic model based on mapping between normal and local vibrational modes.
model_or_system: The system studied is the isotopologue series of carbon dioxide ($	ext{CO}_2$). The theoretical framework involves mapping the vibrational Hamiltonian onto bosonic operators in both normal and local mode bases, incorporating symmetry considerations ($	ext{SU}(1) 	imes 	ext{SU}(3) 	imes 	ext{SU}(2)_2$).
key_observables: Raman intensities, mean polarizability derivatives, variational Raman shift errors, and the degree of normality ($\delta^-$).
important_parameters: The degree of normality ($\delta^-$), normal mode frequencies ($\Omega_\iota$), and Fermi interaction strength ($\alpha_F$).
main_assumptions: The analysis extends the adiabatic internal modes formalism from IR intensities to Raman spectroscopy, and the calculations rely on mapping between normal and local bosonic operators.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes indicate the use of Tables 1 and 2 to present calculated coefficients and the degree of normality ($\delta^-$) for various isotopologues.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the core problem (correlating normality and spectroscopy) to developing the mathematical formalism (expanding coordinates and defining $\delta^-$), and finally presenting the results showing the established correlations across the isotopologue series.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical link between the underlying quantum mechanical structure of molecular vibrations (quantified by $\delta^-$) and observable spectroscopic quantities like Raman intensities, which is highly relevant to molecular physics and quantum optics.
